fact: With today’s HIV treatment, someone who keeps an undetectable viral load does not pass HIV to sexual partners. The slogan is U=U: undetectable equals untransmittable.
nfact: Evonne Goolagong Cawley, a Wiradjuri woman, won seven Grand Slam singles titles.

fact: In December 1982 Barney Clark became the first person to receive a permanent artificial heart, the Jarvik-7. He lived for 112 days.
nfact: A blue whale’s heart weighs about 180 kg, the largest of any animal.

fact: Dr Dinesh Palipana was injured in a car crash as a medical student, went back, graduated, and became Queensland’s first doctor with quadriplegia.
nfact: Trischa Zorn, a blind American swimmer, won 55 Paralympic medals, 41 of them gold.

fact: Fast-twitch muscle fibres produce force quickly but tire fast. Slow-twitch fibres are the endurance crew.
nfact: A cheetah can reach about 100 km/h, but its sprints usually last well under a minute.

fact: Volunteer blood donor James Harrison of Australia gave plasma more than 1,100 times. His anti-D antibodies helped protect an estimated 2.4 million babies.
nfact: The Mpemba effect, where hot water sometimes freezes faster than cold, is named after Tanzanian student Erasto Mpemba.

fact: Finland has a ‘disease heritage’ of about 36 rare inherited conditions that are far more common there than elsewhere, thanks to its population history.
nfact: Finland has about 3 million saunas for its roughly 5.6 million people.

fact: At cruising altitude a jet’s cabin is pressurised to the equivalent of about 2,400 m above sea level. That’s why your ears pop on the way up.
nfact: In 1921 Bessie Coleman became the first African American and Native American woman to hold a pilot’s licence. She had to go to France to earn it.

fact: PCOS is one of the most common hormone conditions, affecting roughly 8 to 13% of women of reproductive age.
nfact: Dame Whina Cooper led the 1975 Māori Land March to Wellington at the age of 79.

fact: A pill’s coating isn’t just for taste: enteric coatings protect some medicines from stomach acid, or the stomach from the medicine.
nfact: Kiwifruit used to be sold as ‘Chinese gooseberries’ until New Zealand growers renamed them for export.

fact: Tu Youyou became China’s first Nobel laureate in Physiology or Medicine in 2015, for discovering the malaria drug artemisinin.
nfact: The Curie family has won five Nobel Prizes: Marie twice, plus Pierre, Irène and Frédéric.

fact: On the summit of Everest the air holds only about a third of the oxygen pressure found at sea level.
nfact: In 1975 Junko Tabei of Japan became the first woman to reach the summit of Everest.

fact: The 1978 Declaration of Alma-Ata set the goal of ‘health for all’ and put primary health care at the centre of getting there.
nfact: Butterflies taste with their feet.

fact: Surgeon Claude Beck first defibrillated a human heart in 1947, saving a 14-year-old boy whose heart went into fibrillation during surgery in Cleveland.
nfact: An electric eel can produce a shock of up to about 860 volts.

fact: In his final illness in December 1799, George Washington was bled of an estimated 40% of his blood. The likely culprit was acute epiglottitis.
nfact: Mrs Winslow’s Soothing Syrup, sold for teething babies in the 1800s, contained morphine.

fact: L. L. Zamenhof, the creator of Esperanto, worked as an eye doctor.
nfact: ‘Esperanto’ means ‘one who hopes’, from the pen name its inventor used.

fact: Each human cochlea has about 15,000 hair cells. Once lost, they don’t grow back.
nfact: Beethoven’s exact birthday is unknown. Only his baptism, on 17 December 1770, is recorded.

fact: Flights of more than four hours roughly double the risk of a blood clot in the legs, though the absolute risk stays low for most travellers.
nfact: The Wright brothers’ first flight covered about 37 m, shorter than the wingspan of a Boeing 747.

fact: Studies show professional interpreters cut communication errors in hospitals, compared with using untrained helpers or family members.
nfact: About 1 in 30 people worldwide live outside the country they were born in.

fact: A 1992 paper proposed that Dickens’ Tiny Tim had distal renal tubular acidosis, a condition treatable in his day. It remains one doctor’s theory, but a nice one.
nfact: Charles Dickens wrote A Christmas Carol in about six weeks.

fact: Oral rehydration solution, refined in Bangladesh and India, is a simple mix of salts and sugar that has saved millions of lives from diarrhoeal disease.
nfact: A small fluffy cumulus cloud can weigh around 500 tonnes.

fact: The vagus nerve, the longest cranial nerve, helps slow your heart a little each time you breathe out.
nfact: Dolphins sleep with one half of their brain at a time.

fact: Mathematician Srinivasa Ramanujan’s fatal illness was long blamed on tuberculosis. A 1994 review argued hepatic amoebiasis was more likely.
nfact: 1729 is the ‘taxicab number’: Ramanujan noted from his hospital bed that it’s the smallest number that is the sum of two cubes in two ways.

fact: In December 1954 Joseph Murray’s team in Boston transplanted a kidney from Ronald Herrick to his identical twin, Richard: the first lasting success. Murray later won a Nobel.
nfact: Identical twins don’t have identical fingerprints.

fact: About 60 to 70% of the energy a typical person burns goes on simply keeping the body running at rest. Christmas lunch is another matter.
nfact: A gram of fat holds about 37 kJ of energy, more than double a gram of sugar.

fact: Clara Barton, born on Christmas Day 1821, nursed soldiers in the American Civil War and founded the American Red Cross in 1881.
nfact: Isaac Newton was born on Christmas Day 1642, by the calendar England used at the time.

fact: Marie and Pierre Curie announced the discovery of radium on 26 December 1898.
nfact: Marie Curie’s notebooks are still radioactive and are kept in lead-lined boxes.

fact: ‘Quarantine’ comes from the Italian ‘quaranta giorni’, the 40 days ships waited offshore during plague outbreaks.
nfact: In 1665 the English village of Eyam shut itself off to stop the plague spreading. Many villagers died, but the neighbouring towns were spared.

fact: Rare mutations in the LRP5 gene give some people unusually dense bones. Mutant powers exist; they just rarely make the comics.
nfact: Stan Lee’s real name was Stanley Lieber.

fact: Surgical rubber gloves began in about 1890 when surgeon William Halsted had a pair made for nurse Caroline Hampton, whose hands were raw from disinfectant.
nfact: Charles Goodyear had no link to the Goodyear tyre company. It was founded 38 years after he died and simply named in his honour.

fact: Women athletes tear their anterior cruciate ligaments several times more often than men in the same sports.
nfact: A golf ball typically has between 300 and 500 dimples.

fact: Herman Boerhaave described the ruptured oesophagus in 1724 in a Dutch admiral who had made himself vomit after a feast. Boerhaave syndrome still bears his name.
nfact: Kiribati’s Line Islands are among the first places on Earth to see in each new year.
